item.title: 3 Ways Emotionally Intelligent People Keep Drama Away
item.description:
Emotional Intelligence

3 Ways Emotionally Intelligent People Keep Drama Away

Delaying gratification can keep drama at bay.

Posted September 6, 2026

Key points
  • Emotionally intelligent people avoid petty power struggles to minimize unnecessary drama.
  • Delaying gratification helps EI individuals prioritize meaningful goals over fleeting desires.
  • Practicing gratitude reduces conflict and fosters more harmonious relationships.

Emotionally intelligent individuals tend to dodge unnecessary drama by doing three things. They avoid petty power struggles, delay gratification, and always seem to have gratitude. Although these tendencies seem simple, they require a person to have self-discipline, a modest ego, and an ability to think, in meaningful ways, about the big picture.

Why Avoiding Petty Power Struggles Is Crucial

Avoiding petty power struggles is a feat. Disagreements with friends, colleagues, or family members about plans, time frames, or opinions about trivial things can test our patience and our ego strength. During these interactions, the person you are dealing with may “hit below the belt” to rattle you so they can gain the upper hand.

For example, on the first Tuesday of every month, you order lunch for your team at work. Your boss graciously picks up the tab, so you are mindful of the expense. The local Thai restaurant seems to be everyone’s favorite, including yours, and is reasonably priced. As you are putting in the order, your co-worker enters your office and says she and the entire team want sushi. You are dubious about this, but she insists. She acts like she is joking around and refers to you as a “suck up” while also insinuating that you are subpar at your job.

Although you are blindsided by the hurtful comments, you recognize that they are mischaracterizations, so you let them go. In your mind, immature people say immature things to disarm your confidence. You refrain from debating with her about the issue, and you order the sushi. Evading an elongated and painful conversation about what to order for lunch, and why her comments are unfair (which she may never see), leaves you with enough time to put the finishing touches on your important project before lunch.

Why Arguing Over Trivial Matters Leads to More Drama

Let’s face it, people who must always get their way and will debate a trivial matter for hours, or overpower people to get what they want, are missing the point of life. There are more important things to focus on, like putting a brilliant finish on an important work task. EI individuals who consider a deeper meaning and do not spend their time arguing about superficial things often have less drama. Moreover, confronting toxic comments may be fruitless because they are typically spoken by an individual who lacks self-awareness and empathy. Addressing it only gives their words more power.

Delaying immediate gratification is also imperative. An individual who can show self-restraint regarding pleasurable activities, usually understands and considers more meaningful priorities. They think deeply about how a self-focused act can impact those around them. Their empathy and consideration usually keeps their relationships healthy and without constant drama. And when the time arrives for them to treat themselves, they relish it even more.

Self-Restraint and Prioritizing Family Needs

For example, Lisa is a newly single mom. Her favorite purchase in autumn is fall boots. She spots the perfect pair but realizes that they are out of her budget. She thinks about the credit card in her wallet. She has just enough credit available to cover an emergency for herself and her kids if it occurs. Although she is tempted to buy the amazing boots, she decides against it and leaves the store. To her, having the ability to take care of her kids outweighs her passion for footwear and her need to be admired by her friends. She goes home and buffs up her old boots and is proud of herself for being a responsible mom.

Remaining grateful is also an emotionally intelligent trait. The EI person may have to mourn a disappointment or loss, but after they do, they quickly identify the positives about the situation. In addition, EI folks rarely take people for granted. They are exceedingly aware of what others do for them and seem to routinely provide “thanks” to the people in their life. They operate from a position of positivity, and it is not fake. They reflect and understand even the small blessings that bring them peace and contentment. Because they are grateful, and the people around them know that they are, there is less conflict. Conversely, an individual who perpetually feels like their life is harder than everyone else’s and feels like the people around them should be catering to them, cannot always transcend from a difficult time to a better time because they are entrenched in feeling sorry for themselves.

Although drama (conflict) is a part of every relationship, there are ways that EI people, largely, keep it at bay. Taking the high road instead of engaging in petty power struggles, limiting their selfish acts if it impacts loved ones, and always reminding themselves of what they have in place of what they do not, are ways that they keep their relationships relatively peaceful. You can find more information on this topic in my book, How to Outsmart a Narcissist, Use Emotional Intelligence to Regain Control at Home, work, and In Life.

item.title: Coolness and Autonomy: The Paradox of Trying Too Hard
item.description:
Memes

Coolness and Autonomy: The Paradox of Trying Too Hard

People who appear effortlessly independent often earn the most status.

Posted September 6, 2026

Key points
  • Trying to seem cool betrays the very need for approval that coolness is supposed to signal away.
  • Research suggests that magnetism comes from absorption in the work, not from a strategy aimed at the audience.
  • Mimicking or rebelling against social desires both signal dependence on others' opinions.

On the set of The Thomas Crown Affair, director Norman Jewison became increasingly frustrated with his star actor Steve McQueen. Jewison kept imploring him to play the role with more visible charisma, more swagger. McQueen refused. He underplayed everything. He let silences hang. He did less when the script called for more.

Trying to be cool, all too easily backfires
Source: malay via UnSplash

Jewison's frustration reportedly reached a boiling point just before he watched the dailies. It was then that he could see that McQueen, by refusing to perform coolness, had become the most magnetic thing on screen. It wasn't a technique or performance. He seemed constitutionally uninterested in trying to impress anyone, and that particular quality, that specific absence, turned out to be the thing nobody could look away from.

We recognize this dynamic instantly when we see it. The person at the party trying too hard to seem indifferent, the band making a show of not caring about record sales, the startup founder who won't stop telling you how little they care about what VCs think. An obvious attempt to seem cool and detached is its own kind of neediness, and everyone can feel it. As Luke Burgis, the author of The One and the Ninety-Nine observed in a recent conversation, "There's a danger in a kid in high school who's trying way too hard to be cool. It just doesn't work like that."

We get this intuitively. But the question is why? What is it about the conscious attempt at creative independence that undermines itself? What is the psychology of cool? And if you can't try your way into it, where does the real thing actually come from?

The Psychology of Cool

Coolness, despite feeling like a vague cultural term, turns out to be a surprisingly specific, well-studied psychological phenomenon. Caleb Warren at the University of Arizona has spent years investigating what it actually consists of, and his research identifies a remarkably consistent factor: perceived autonomy. People and things are seen as cool when they diverge from norms in ways that feel self-directed and appropriate. You don't come off as cool by flouting every convention in sight. There's important nuance there. You're perceived as cool by deviating from the ones that feel unnecessary, and crucially, in ways that seem to come naturally.

And here's the finding that matters most for our purposes. Warren and his team found that people earn less status when they visibly try to be cool compared to when coolness appears effortless. The act of trying betrays the very dependence on others' approval that coolness is supposed to signal the absence of. Put simply: you cannot try your way into being cool.

article continues after advertisement

Cool Meets The Psychology of Mimetic Desire

René Girard, the Stanford philosopher behind mimetic theory, offers a framework for understanding why. Girard's central insight is that human desire is fundamentally social. When our basic needs are met, we look to our social group to determine what we want. Desire begets desire. Most desire, in Girard's view, is borrowed.

The cool factor is deeply related to mimetic desire
Source: Chanaan Greenblat

This is the engine of audience capture. Pop artists, fast fashion brands, market-driven companies: they all swim in this web of borrowed desire, tracking what people want and adjusting accordingly. The rare figures who appear to desire independently of the social current become enormously attractive precisely because they seem to operate on a private frequency.

But Burgis, whose first book, Wanting, builds extensively on Girard's, identifies a trap. Consciously setting out to be anti-mimetic is still a form of orientation toward the crowd. You're doing the opposite of what you think they want, which is still a reaction, still downstream of the audience's preferences. The conscious resistance to the crowd presupposes a fixation on the crowd. You can't push against something without first bracing yourself against it.

Audience Capture and The Psychology of Cool

The figures who actually escape this trap share something in common, and it has little to do with strategy. They're absorbed in their medium to a degree that crowds out the question of the audience entirely.

Burgis, in his book, explores this through Ornette Coleman. Coleman didn't set out to invent free jazz. He was working in a department store when, during his lunch break, he wandered into a gallery and saw a painting of a wealthy woman with "the most solitary expression in the world." He went home and wrote "Lonely Woman," a song that would eventually break the genre open. The originality was a byproduct of absorption, not a goal. His contemporary Miles Davis expressed a similar sentiment: "It's always been a gift with me, hearing music the way I do. I don't know where it comes from, it's just there and I don't question it."

Jazz provides an insightful window into the psychology of cool
Source: Swello via UnSplash

These are people so consumed by their material that the question of the audience simply doesn't arise. In a recent conversation, Burgis described this as a kind of productive forgetfulness: the best creative work happens when "you kind of just forget" the audience exists.

Not Trying to be Cool

It's worth noting, of course, that being independent of one's audience guarantees nothing. You can ignore the audience completely and still produce work nobody values. Coleman experienced this himself, spending almost a decade in poverty. There are no assurances here, only uncertainty.

article continues after advertisement

What gives these figures their gravitational pull isn't simply the absence of concern for others. It's the presence of something far more powerful: a fascination with the material that runs so deep it crowds out the need for approval entirely. They aren't trying to be cool, or anti-mimetic, or to be perceived in any particular way. And that, paradoxically, is what gives certain people that gravitational pull.

Norman Jewison didn't understand what McQueen was doing until he watched the footage. On set, it looked like a refusal. On screen, it looked like magnetism. McQueen was uninterested in performing at all. He had his own idea of how the role should be played, and he was more absorbed in that vision than in what the director, the studio, or the audience expected of him.

item.title: The Case for Getting a Little Lost
item.description:
Memory

The Case for Getting a Little Lost

New research suggests finding your way may build skills GPS can’t replace.

Posted September 6, 2026

Key points
  • A 2025 study suggests that the brain's navigation system doesn't work like GPS.
  • Heavier GPS use predicted worse spatial memory years later.
  • Kids allowed to roam farther without adults report lower wayfinding anxiety as adults.
Getting a little lost may be more necessary than ever
Source: Pexels, Allan Mas

I used to keep getting lost until I turned on GPS. Then, I got lost only rarely, and more specifically, when there was recent construction on the road and the GPS got confused. But then, once, after I had come to rely almost exclusively on GPS and my battery died, I got lost, and I didn't have the skills to recover. “Where am I?” I wondered, looking out at an unfamiliar landscape. Over time, I noticed, I was paying less attention to the landscape as well, assuming the GPS was doing the work for me.

What I had noticed in myself turns out to have a neurological counterpart. A recent study found it by looking at what happens in the brains of mice as they move through space.

For decades, we’ve assumed that the brain’s navigation system operates similarly to an internal GPS. We ask for directions internally, and the system responds, telling us “north” or “northwest.” But a team at the German Cancer Research Center, led by Hannah Monyer and Kevin Allen, has found that the analogy may be wrong. GPS and our internal navigation systems seem more different than alike.

In their study, the researchers recorded from more than 10 grid cells at once in mice moving around freely, then used a model to read their direction and speed from the pattern of neurons. While GPS relies on a fixed reference system, grid cells can switch between reference frames, such as a wall or a landmark, as the animal moves. Without reliable cues to correct against, the animal’s sense of direction can gradually drift even while it remains confident about where it is.

Implications for Alzheimer's Disease and Navigation Skills

Monyer thinks this may help explain why people with Alzheimer's lose their bearings. Equally, this research direction raises the question: Could changes in navigation skills eventually help detect Alzheimer's earlier?

Cultural anthropologist Claudio Aporta noticed a similar distinction while studying navigation and the introduction of GPS in the Canadian Arctic. Earlier tools, including maps and dead reckoning, still required people to maintain some internal sense of their position as they traveled. Turn-by-turn GPS doesn’t work the same; you can arrive at the right place without building much of a mental representation of the route. As Aporta put it when I interviewed him, “What kind of decisions are you not making when something is telling you everything you need to know?”

Other studies of GPS have started to draw closer links between GPS use and spatial memory. In a 2020 study, McGill researchers assessed 50 drivers' GPS habits and spatial memory, then retested 13 of them three years later. In that follow-up, they found that people who had relied more heavily on GPS showed larger declines in their ability to navigate without it, as compared with lighter GPS users. The order matters here: Greater GPS use came first and predicted poorer navigation later. It wasn’t simply that people with worse spatial memory had begun relying more heavily on GPS because they already felt lost.

article continues after advertisement

The study was a small one, and it’s important not to overgeneralize. But if these findings hold up, the implications extend beyond adults who have gotten used to following a blue line on a screen. My own kids, ages 9 and 14, are at the age when this reliance on GPS starts to matter.

How Children Develop Spatial Navigation Skills

As children develop, they start navigating less by individual memorized turns—for example, left at the gas station or right at the church—and begin forming a fuller sense of a place as a whole. But in order to develop that fuller sense, they need to get lost and make wrong turns. They need to have that moment—or many moments, really—when they think, “Oh, that’s not right at all.”

A 2020 study gives this a sharper edge. College students reported how far they'd been allowed to roam without adults as kids. Farther roaming as kids meant lower wayfinding anxiety as adults, and that held up even after controlling for general anxiety. Simply spending more time outside didn't produce the same effect, but the distance they had been allowed to travel without adults did.

Learning how to recover when you are unsure where you are may also teach you that being unsure is something you can handle.

The decline in independent navigation isn't new. British researcher Mayer Hillman found in 1990 that the number of 7-year-olds walking to school alone in England had dropped from over 70% in 1971 to under 10%. When you compare the generations, you see a similar difference. Specifically, among kids born around 1990, only about 9% were walking to school alone at 10 or 11 years old, compared with around 40% of kids that age born roughly 50 to 60 years earlier.

And that lack of independence can influence how we parent. As one study found, parents who had less freedom to navigate on their own as kids tend to give their own kids less of that same freedom.

Balancing Safety, Equity, and Independence in Child Navigation

I’m not suggesting we stop supervising kids. Many towns have become more urban and more difficult to navigate, and there are dangers we can’t afford to ignore. There’s clearly an equity issue as well; some families and children don’t live in places where it’s especially safe to walk alone. In part in response, some schools have started walking school buses: a rotating group of parents walks a fixed route, picking up kids along the way. Nobody walks alone or gets driven, and kids still learn the streets.

article continues after advertisement

Practices like these give children a chance to notice when they’ve taken a wrong turn and figure out how to correct it in real-time. The whole system—mine, yours, and the mouse's—was built to notice when it's wrong and fix itself. It was never built to be told the answer every single time.
